title: IAM Security Best Practices
subtopics: Rotating and revoking credentials when appropriate
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of iam security best practices and its relationship to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to iam security best practices.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn iam security best practices in the context of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: IAM Security Best Practices matters because it is one part of aws identity and access management. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: IAM permission evaluation
content_blocks.alt_text: Authorization depends on identity and resource policies, applicable boundaries/organization controls, conditions, and explicit denies.
content_blocks.caption: Default deny applies; an applicable explicit deny overrides an allow.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** IAM Security Best Practices belongs to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM answers who can do what to which resource under which conditions. Prefer federated human access and temporary workload credentials; grant only what the job needs.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Root-user protection; MFA and secure authentication; Avoiding embedded access keys; Rotating and revoking credentials when appropriate. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For iam security best practices, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Root-user protection
items.text: State the principal, action, resource and applicable conditions. Prefer scoped permissions and temporary credentials, protect secrets, and collect evidence that access is both limited and usable.

items.title: MFA and secure authentication
items.text: State the principal, action, resource and applicable conditions. Prefer scoped permissions and temporary credentials, protect secrets, and collect evidence that access is both limited and usable.

items.title: Avoiding embedded access keys
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: Rotating and revoking credentials when appropriate
items.text: State the principal, action, resource and applicable conditions. Prefer scoped permissions and temporary credentials, protect secrets, and collect evidence that access is both limited and usable.

content_blocks.title: Permission-evaluation order: IAM Security Best Practices
content_blocks.code:
1. Identify the principal and requested action/resource.
2. Collect applicable identity/resource policies and controls.
3. Evaluate conditions and boundaries.
4. Any applicable explicit Deny wins; otherwise an applicable Allow is required.
content_blocks.expected_output: A repeatable troubleshooting sequence rather than a guarantee that a single policy controls access.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “IAM Security Best Practices”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for IAM Security Best Practices with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: IAM Security Best Practices is taught as part of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
IAM answers who can do what to which resource under which conditions. Prefer federated human access and temporary workload credentials; grant only what the job needs.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
